title: Prediction: under GRH the 'sign layer' reaches n(p) ≤ 2 log² p, so if s(p) were a function of n(p) alone ES would follow — the data say it is not alone
connection: Bach's bound makes character patterns of p escape square-like behaviour by ℓ ≈ 2 log² p. If ES-hardness were controlled only by n(p) (plus bounded noise), a GRH-conditional pointwise argument would exist. The observed n(p) = 17 record with s = 2814 shows extra (class-layer) difficulty — consistent with the campaign's 'class, not parity' gap.
why: Separates how much of ES's tail is explained by the sign layer (characters) vs the class layer; quantitative version of FRONTIER's F6/G4 split.
first_step: Quantify: fraction of variance of log s(p) explained by the quadratic-character vector of p modulo ℓ ≤ 100 (linear/tree model).

title: U(p) at least-QNR-record primes is only moderately small
connection: At the least p≡1(4) with least QNR q (q=11..47), U(p)/log²p = 0.40,0.37,0.54,0.53,0.36,0.29,0.60,0.53,0.55,0.67,0.61 — below typical (≈1–2) but not record-hard; 2521 (least QNR 11) is far harder (0.15).
why: Shows hardness is not a function of the least QNR alone: p−1 smoothness / p ≡ 1 mod higher prime powers adds a second axis — useful for designing a two-parameter hardness model.
first_step: Regress log U(p) on log L(1,χ_p) and log(σ(p−1)/(p−1)) jointly; check which explains 2521 vs 87481.

title: minlcm(p)/p at primes not in OEIS; correlates +0.23 with least QNR
connection: The least common denominator over solutions, divided by p, behaves like a cost: larger when small primes are QRs (ρ=+0.23 with least QNR, +0.20 with L(1,χ_p)).
why: Smallest common denominator = smallest N with 4N/p a sum of three divisors of N (Egyptian-fraction 'practical number' view) — links ES to practical numbers / Erdős–Graham denominators.
first_step: Check: is minlcm(p)/p always a practical number? Compute and compare to OEIS A005153.

title: U(n) records at 2,3,6,8,10,12,15,24,30,40,48,60,… vs highly composite numbers
connection: Record positions of U(n) (not in OEIS) are dominated by smooth numbers but are not A002182 (15, 30, 40 appear; 36 does not).
why: Records of a divisor-sum-like count should track the extremal order of a specific divisor function; identifying it gives the right 'max U(n) ≍ ?' growth.
first_step: Compare record positions with records of Σ_{d|n} τ(d)², τ(n)τ(n+1)…; fit max_{n≤X} U(n) vs exp(c log X/log log X).

title: Easy primes: U(p) records eventually all ≡ −1 (mod 840)
why: Mirror of the hard primes (≡ 1 mod 840): ES-easiest primes are ≡ −1 modulo highly composite numbers (5039 = 7! − 1 = 2·2520 − 1). The count is a function of p's position relative to smooth numbers.
first_step: Note 55439 = 2·27720 − 1 and 5039 = 2·2520 − 1 are records; test the next candidates 2·lcm(1..k) − 1 and lcm(1..k) − 1 when prime; OEIS search of the record list gave no match.
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0037] Check if record primes satisfy p+1 = smooth with record τ(p+1); OEIS search of the record list (no match).

title: maxx(p) − p/4 (largest smallest-denominator)
connection: The largest possible smallest denominator maxx(p) has maxx − p/4 weakly tied to least QNR (ρ=−0.19); maxx(p) ≤ 3p/4 always; the sequence is not in OEIS.
why: Measures how 'balanced' the most balanced solution can be (BALANCED_LATTICE.md); balanced solutions are rare and relate to the cubic surface's real-point distribution.
first_step: Plot (maxx(p) − p/4)/p; compare with the balanced-solution census in BALANCED_LATTICE.md.

title: R(3^k) = 0 exactly for even k (squares) and k = 1
why: Sanity fingerprint of T1 on prime powers; also the odd-power values (2,2,4,18,10,10) are a small test sequence for any closed formula.
first_step: Compare R(3^{2j+1}) with the BM main term M_BM(3^{2j+1}).

title: W(n) (all words) has records at 1,3,5,7,11,17,19,23,35,47,59,71,…
connection: Records of W(n) = #{t,u,v ≥ 1 : tuv−u−v = n} are at n with n+1 and 2n+1, 3n+1… all highly divisible (W counts divisors of tn+1 in classes); not in OEIS.
why: W(n) = Σ_t #{d | tn+1 : d ≡ −1 (mod t)} is the unrestricted analogue of the ES certificate count — its extremal behaviour bounds all sub-counts.
first_step: Identify W(n) with a classical divisor-sum (Σ_t τ_{−1 mod t}(tn+1)); submit to OEIS.

title: Euler-product weights per prime q for log U(p)
connection: Fit log U(p) residual = Σ_q β_q χ_p(q) for q ≤ 50 (at p ≡ 1 (4), χ_{−4p}(q) = (−1/q)χ_p(q) is collinear, so a joint χ_p/χ_{−4p} per-q fit is unidentifiable — only one coefficient per q is meaningful).
why: The fitted β_q, γ_q profile is a 'local-density fingerprint' that a heuristic count (Elsholtz–Tao style) should reproduce exactly; mismatches pinpoint missing local factors.
first_step: Done in data/z52b/qweights.json (χ_p only); compare β_q with −c/q (naive Euler factor slope).

title: Variance of log U(p) after removing the χ_p effect: what is left?
connection: After the Euler-product fit (R² gain ≈ 0.49), the remaining residual variance can be tested against τ((p+3)/4), τ(p−1), and pure noise.
why: Quantifies how much of ES count fluctuation is 'genuinely global' (divisor coincidences) vs local — the global part is what any proof must control pointwise.
first_step: Fit the full model log U ~ log p + Euler(χ_p) + Euler(χ_{−4p}) + log τ((p+3)/4) + log τ(p−1) and report residual variance.

title: ES counts at Sophie Germain / safe primes
connection: Safe primes (p = 2q+1) have p−1 maximally non-smooth; predicted to be ES-easy. Compute mean U(p)/log²p over safe primes vs all primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) (safe primes > 7 are ≡ 3 (mod 4)… so compare within class).
why: Tests the p−1 smoothness axis independent of p mod 4 (within p ≡ 3 (4), which is always ES-easy but count still varies).
first_step: Compute on p ≡ 3 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵: ρ(U, P⁺(p−1)) and mean over safe primes.

title: p mod 5 and p mod 7 as integers are uninformative (|ρ| ≤ 0.07)
connection: Raw residues p mod 5, p mod 7 show tiny correlation; the information is in the Legendre symbols (5/p), (7/p) (and for 7 even that is null).
why: Sanity: ES local dependence is via characters, not the residue's numeric value.
first_step: None.

title: Number of distinct x vs number of solutions per x: concentration index
connection: U(p)/nx(p) (solutions per first denominator) is a concentration fingerprint; Gini coefficient of the x-profile per prime.
why: If solutions concentrate on few x, ES at p reduces to few divisor problems — relevant to POINTWISE strategies.
first_step: Compute U/nx at p ≤ 2·10⁵ (both in data) and its dependence on χ_p.

title: Linear-algebra fingerprint: rank of the solution set's denominator matrix mod small primes
connection: For each p, collect (x,y,z) mod q (q = 3, 5, 7) of all solutions; the occupied residue patterns form a fingerprint; compare across hard and easy primes.
why: Local solution patterns at q are exactly what covering congruences use; hard primes should occupy few patterns.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁴ (needs solution lists — extend the counter to dump solutions).

title: U(p) for p ≡ 3 (4): correlation profile mirrors p ≡ 1 (4)?
connection: All correlations above were computed for p ≡ 1 (4); for p ≡ 3 (4) ES is trivial but counts still fluctuate — compare the χ_p fit.
why: If the same Euler-product law holds, the count law is uniform across classes — a sign it comes from the surface's local densities, not from ES-specific structure.
first_step: Rerun z52b_fingerprint_lfit.py restricted to p ≡ 3 (4).

title: Composite n: is U(n) multiplicative-ish? (U(pq) vs U(p), U(q))
connection: Compute-and-check: for n = pq ≤ 30 000, regress log U(pq) on log U(p), log U(q).
why: ES for composites is inherited from prime factors; quantifying how the count lifts tells whether the 'solution sheaf' is multiplicative.
first_step: Use f4_all_30000.txt; scatter log U(pq) − log U(p) − log U(q).

title: U(p²) and U(p³): prime powers fingerprint
connection: Compute U at prime squares and cubes (in range: p² ≤ 30 000): odd squares kill all certificate lines (T1) but ES(p²) holds via p — how big is U(p²)?
why: T1 says line counts vanish at squares; U(p²) shows how many 'non-line' solutions exist — a measure of what T1-avoiding methods must capture.
first_step: Extract U(m²) for odd m ≤ 173 from the data and compare with U at neighbouring non-squares.

title: Hard-prime 'deficit vectors' over local primes
connection: For each hard prime compute the vector ((q/p))_{q≤47} and 1[q | p+3], 1[q | p−1]; cluster hard primes by these vectors.
why: If hard primes form a few clusters (e.g. 'all small q QR' and 'p−1 smooth'), each cluster may need a different certificate family.
first_step: k-means on the 200 hardest primes ≤ 2·10⁵ with these binary features.

title: x | z ⟺ y | z for every solution at a prime (proved from the normal form)
connection: Since p | z, 4z/p = z/x + z/y + 1 is an integer identity: if x | z then z/y is an integer, and conversely. Data agree (identical failure sets and share 0.377).
why: Suggests a structural lemma: at a prime, x | z forces y | z (and conversely), i.e. z = lcm(x, y) — a rigid sub-family amenable to a parametrisation by divisors of z/p.
first_step: Use the lcm-closed family z = lcm(x, y) as a parametrisation by divisors of z/p (three divisors a, b of z with a + b + 1 = 4z/p).

title: Full chain x | y | z fails at 670 primes ≤ 10⁵, starting 73, 193, 313, 337, 409, 457, 577, …
connection: Chains exist for most primes but fail at a sizeable set containing the hard primes 193, 409, 577, 1201 (not in OEIS).
why: The chain sub-family is a 1-parameter-poorer certificate; its failure set is a hardness filter between the full ES and single lines.
first_step: Compute the density of chain failures among p ≡ 1 (24) vs others; is it ≈ constant (then infinitely many failures) or decaying?

title: Solutions with x prime fail at 4 597 primes; with some perfect-square denominator at 3 134
connection: Prime smallest denominators (share 0.7%) and square denominators (0.8%) are rare; failure sets start 31, 37, 53, 73, … and 17, 29, 41, 73, 89, … (no OEIS match).
why: Rare-shape sub-families give no ES leverage but are fingerprints for 'random-like' behaviour of denominators (density of primes/squares among x).
first_step: Compare the share of prime x with 1/log x heuristics (≈ 1/log(p/4)).

title: 'Only z divisible by n' fails at all powers of 2 (composites ≤ 3000)
connection: At n = 2^k every solution has ≥ 2 denominators divisible by n (or none); at odd primes the k₁-shape always exists.
why: Powers of 2 are the ES 'easy' case but structurally degenerate; sanity fingerprint for the normal-form lemma.
first_step: None.

title: Predict per-prime weights β_q from the BM main term
connection: M_BM(p) = Σ (1 − (−uB/p))/φ(4uB): expanding (−uB/p) = ∏_{q|uB} (q/p)^{v_q} predicts how each (q/p) shifts the mean count; compare with q·β_q ≈ −0.35 for q ≡ 2 (3) and the q ≡ 1 (3) confound.
why: A quantitative match would show the BM term is the full explanation of the χ_p fluctuations of U; a mismatch identifies missing terms (e.g. the shift couplings via (−s/q)).
first_step: Compute ∂ E[M_BM | (q/p) = ±1] numerically at p ≤ 30 000 for each q ≤ 47 and plot against fitted β_q.

title: Hard primes vs Wilson / Wolstenholme-type congruences: null test
connection: Wilson quotients (p−1)!+1)/p mod p and Wolstenholme quotients are p-adic invariants of small integers collectively; test correlation with residual U(p).
why: Expected null (ES counts depend on quadratic data); a non-null would be surprising and important.
first_step: Compute Wilson quotient mod p for p ≤ 2·10⁵ (O(p) each — use p ≤ 2·10⁴) and Spearman.

title: U(n) at Sylvester-sequence-related n (2, 3, 7, 43, 1807, …)
connection: Sylvester numbers s_k satisfy 1 = Σ 1/s_i + 1/(s_k − 1); n = 43, 1807 = 13·139: compute U and compare to neighbours.
why: Numbers with built-in unit-fraction identities might have anomalously many ES solutions (an 'easy family' mirror of lcm+1).
first_step: Look up U(43), U(1807) in f4_all_30000.txt; extend to 3263443 = s₅ with the count program.

title: Ramanujan-sum expansion of the normalised ES count
connection: Compute-and-check: least-squares coefficients a_q in U(n)/log³n ≈ Σ_{q ≤ Q} a_q c_q(n) over n ≤ 30 000.
why: If a_q is (nearly) multiplicative with a_p ≈ −1/p-ish, the count has an Euler-product singular series over n — the all-n analogue of the χ_p law at primes.
first_step: Implement c_q(n) = Σ_{d | gcd(q,n)} μ(q/d) d and fit.

title: A392469's empirical bound k(p) < 71 log p vs our certificate-size laws
connection: Gold notes k(a(n)) < 71·log a(n) for all known records; our (★) Cmin has mean ≈ 2 with rare large values (23105 at a boundary case), and Vmin ≤ 116 ≤ 3·10⁶.
why: Logarithmic certificate size is exactly what a 'small-certificate covering' approach needs; comparing the k(p) law with the line-specific laws tells which line has the best size profile.
first_step: Plot max_{p ≤ X} k(p)/log p from mink_pr_2e5.txt and compare with Vmin, Cmin records.

title: A257843 (Hasler): n where the lexicographically first solution ≠ the max-z solution
why: A 'solution-geometry' fingerprint (shape of the solution set's extremes) — a cheap invariant that may separate hard from easy classes.
first_step: Compute the density of A257843 among p ≡ 1 (24) vs others and correlate membership with residual U(p).

title: Lowest-count composites: are they products of hard primes?
connection: Rank composite n ≤ 30 000 by U(n)/log³n; test whether the lowest are products of two primes both in the hard class (p ≡ 1 mod 24) such as 73·193.
why: If hardness multiplies, composite ES-hardness reduces to prime hardness (expected: composites inherit solutions from each factor, so they should be easy).
first_step: Sort f4_all_30000.txt by U/log³n restricted to composites.

title: ES count vs number of prime factors ≡ 1 (mod 4) of n
connection: For composite n, fit log U(n) on ω₁(n) = #{p | n : p ≡ 1 (4)} and ω₃(n); the isosceles law says ω₃ = 0 kills degenerate solutions for odd n (even n have them anyway); does ω₃ also boost the bulk count?
why: Quantifies how the 'sum of two squares' structure of n influences ES counts beyond the isosceles locus.
first_step: Regress on f4_all_30000.txt.

title: Ratio y/x and z/y spectra as fingerprints of identity families
connection: Polynomial identity families produce solutions with rational ratios y/x → constants as p grows (e.g. y ≈ 2x); peaks in the empirical distribution of y/x identify which identities fire.
why: A data-driven way to rediscover Mordell-type identities and to see which ones the hard classes lack.
first_step: Histogram log(y/x) over all solutions at p ≤ 2·10⁵ split by class mod 840.

title: Hard-prime 'twin' structure: p and p + 2520 both hard?
connection: Because hardness depends on p mod 840 and quadratic characters, p and p + 840k share the mod-840 part but not the characters at q ∤ 840; test correlation of residuals at lag 840 among primes.
why: Separates the periodic (mod 840) from the character part: lag-840 correlation among primes estimates their variance shares (cf. 0.60 autocorrelation over all n).
first_step: Compute residual correlation for prime pairs (p, p+840k), k ≤ 10.

title: Fingerprint of 'ES at p' vs 'ES at 4p+1' / 'ES at (p+3)/4'
connection: The (★) divisor form involves 4Cp + 1 and the greedy step (p+3)/4; test whether U(4p+1) or U((p+3)/4) (when composite, often easy) correlates with U(p).
why: Cheap check of whether ES difficulty propagates along the natural 'p-tied integer' maps (a dynamical view: forests in FOREST_*.md).
first_step: Compute Spearman(U(p), U(4p+1)) for p ≤ 7 500 and Spearman(U(p), U((p+3)/4)).

title: Near-equal denominator perturbations
connection: Write y=z+h and study the exact residual equation as h varies, connecting ES to near-square factorization.
why: Small h gives structured, checkable subfamilies without claiming they cover every prime.
first_step: Enumerate the smallest attainable difference z−y for primes below 1000.

title: Higher power residue labels
connection: Decorate auxiliary divisors with cubic or quartic residue data to distinguish classes invisible to quadratic symbols.
why: Extra labels might reveal a constructive partition even when they do not force existence.
first_step: For primes in suitable congruence classes, compare certificate frequencies across power-residue labels.

title: Cancellation across auxiliary parameters
connection: Sum character errors over C before taking absolute values, looking for cancellation lost in parameterwise bounds.
why: Different certificate lines may compensate each other's arithmetic biases.
first_step: Compute signed nonprincipal-character contributions for C≤30 over a sample of primes.

title: Local densities as fingerprints
connection: Compute exact residue-level densities for several certificate families and use the vector of densities as a fingerprint of p.
why: Local fingerprints might predict complementary families without asserting a local-global principle.
first_step: Enumerate admissible parameter tuples modulo 8,9,5,7 for three exact identities.

title: Proof-producing set cover
connection: Compress a finite verified range into exact identity templates plus a certified set-cover computation.
why: The output remains a finite-range proof, but it makes coverage mechanisms auditable.
first_step: Take 100 primes and export the chosen identities with exact substitution witnesses for each covered prime.

title: Sunflower patterns among constraints
connection: Search for families of certificate conditions sharing a common core and disjoint extra congruence requirements.
why: A sunflower structure may identify a reusable common lemma with several interchangeable completions.
first_step: Represent each small family by its set of atomic congruence conditions and detect common-core collections.

title: Finite-state rational transducers
connection: Search for digit-wise rules mapping p to candidate denominator digits with bounded carry memory.
why: A successful rule on a well-defined input language could become an explicit infinite family.
first_step: Synthesize a transducer for one already verified congruence family and inspect which extra states are needed to enlarge its domain.

title: Syntax-guided parametrizations
connection: Define a grammar of gcd, floor, product, and reciprocal operations and search short candidate certificate programs.
why: A restricted grammar makes discovery auditable and encourages explicit formulas rather than opaque predictions.
first_step: Enumerate expressions of depth at most three and test exact identities on a training set before symbolic checking.

title: Abstract interpretation of parameters
connection: Propagate intervals, congruence classes, and sign information through a candidate denominator program.
why: A sound abstract domain can prove that many inputs produce positive integers without enumerating them.
first_step: Implement transfer rules for addition, multiplication, and exact division on interval-congruence pairs.

title: Factoring-free gcd certificates
connection: Search for constructions where a useful divisor is produced as a gcd of two explicit expressions.
why: A gcd can supply a verified factor without requiring complete factorization.
first_step: Try short polynomial gcd expressions in p and C and retain only cases where the gcd provably has the target residue.

title: Decision trees as conjecture extractors
connection: Fit shallow trees using residue and character features, then translate each leaf into a proposed arithmetic lemma.
why: A transparent leaf condition is a concrete object for proof or counterexample search.
first_step: Fit a depth-three tree for one family's success and exhaustively test each leaf condition in a larger range.

title: Enumerating low-degree curves on the surface
connection: Search directly for lines or conics contained in a chosen compactification rather than guessing denominator formulas individually.
why: Coefficient equations turn the family search into a finite symbolic problem at each degree.
first_step: Substitute a general affine line with rational coefficients and solve the resulting coefficient equations.

title: Backward construction from a desired last step
connection: Start with the final exact integrality or positivity lemma a certificate proof would need, then solve backward for parameter choices satisfying it.
why: Backward search can produce identities that forward enumeration misses, with every reverse step checked algebraically.
first_step: Choose a target congruence for a complementary divisor, substitute it into the residual equation, and solve for one remaining auxiliary parameter.

title: Self-organized criticality: is the distribution of C_min(p) a power law?
connection: If C_min(p) (first winning C) has a power-law tail, the 'rare hard primes' are scale-free and adversarial search at 10¹⁸ would find larger C_min than seen; if exponential, pointwise proofs 'should' exist with C ≤ (log p)^A.
why: Directly calibrates the shape a proof must take (bounded C ⇒ covering, polylog C ⇒ sieve-like).
first_step: Compute C_min(p) for p ≤ 10⁷ and fit tail; check repo (git grep 'C_min\|smallest c' DISPROOF_AVENUES.md STATUS.md).
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0157] Record, for verification filters, the number of filter stages before a prime is resolved; plot tail distribution.

title: Program synthesis (enumerative/DreamCoder) for a 'solution formula' with branching on residues
connection: Search the space of programs 'if p ≡ r mod M then (x,y,z) = (polynomials in p)' with sqrt/floor allowed (non-polynomial! escaping Mordell–Schinzel) that output a valid ES solution on as many primes as possible.
why: Mordell–Schinzel kills polynomial identities on square classes; identities with floor, gcd, or ⌊√p⌋ are not covered by that theorem and nobody has systematically searched them.
first_step: Define a DSL: polynomials in p, ⌊√p⌋, ⌊p/k⌋, gcd(p+a, b), residue branching; run enumerative search (depth ≤ 6) scoring on primes ≡ 1 mod 840 up to 10⁵; report best coverage.
refs: Mordell–Schinzel (no polynomial identity on square classes)

title: Boolean function analysis: Fourier spectrum of the indicator 'C wins for p' as a function of p mod 4C·something
connection: For fixed C, whether 4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C depends on p via the factorisation of 4Cp+1; its Fourier spectrum over p mod M (M a multiple of 4C) measures 'junta-ness'.
why: A low-degree Fourier concentration for all C would be a covering-ish structure; spectrum spread across high frequencies says the event is genuinely 'global'.
first_step: Compute, for C ≤ 20 and M = lcm(4C, 840), the Fourier spectrum (over ℤ/M) of E_p[win_C(p) | p ≡ r mod M] for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Automated theorem proving on the 'two-term' lemma with a free parameter: Vampire/E on the divisor form
connection: First-order provers can sometimes prove number-theoretic lemmas given axioms about divisibility; the lemma 'if p ≡ 1 mod 24 and p < 2^k then ∃C ≤ K ...' is a bounded statement they might handle for small k.
why: Low chance, but the prover's search traces for small k might reveal which lemmas are reused — a proof-skeleton extraction.
first_step: Encode the divisor form in TPTP with Peano arithmetic axioms + bounded quantifiers; try Vampire for k ≤ 8.

title: Model-checking a finite abstraction: ES for p 'with all small primes' residues fixed' as a finite transition system
connection: Abstract p by its residues mod all primes ≤ B and by its Legendre symbols; a finite-state system over these abstractions can be model-checked for the property 'some C ≤ K yields a divisor in class'. Counterexample traces are candidate hard residue profiles.
why: Finds the exact abstract profile of a potential counterexample; such profiles could then be hunted at 10¹⁸ (adversarial search guidance).
first_step: Enumerate profiles of p mod 840 and Legendre symbols (q/p) for q ≤ 31; for each profile, compute the empirical fraction of primes with C_min ≤ 10; find worst profiles.

title: Bit-level pattern mining on winning C in binary (are winning C's 'smooth'? 'prime'? 'powers of 2'?)
connection: The multiplicative structure of winning C matters (4C is the modulus); test whether winning C are biased toward smooth numbers, primes, or specific residue classes mod 3, 5, 7.
why: A bias (e.g. winning C is often a multiple of 3 for p ≡ 1 mod 3) is a candidate identity direction; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ collect all winning C ≤ 1000; compare their distribution of ω(C), smoothness, C mod 12 against the uniform baseline.

title: De Bruijn / universal cycle: does a single 'universal' residue sequence of C's cover all primes up to X with O(log X) entries?
connection: Hitting-set problem: find the smallest set S of C's such that every prime p ≤ X has a winner in S. Its growth |S(X)| in X (constant? log X? X^ε?) is the 'covering dimension' of ES.
why: If |S(X)| = O(log X) with a nice structure (e.g. S = {1,2,3,6,...} products of small primes), a 'nested cover' proof shape emerges.
first_step: Greedy set-cover on the prime–C incidence matrix for p ≤ 10⁷, C ≤ 10⁴; report |S| vs X.

title: Gaps between consecutive winning C at fixed p: bounded? polylog?
connection: For fixed p, the set of winning C is infinite (e.g. once one C wins, multiples? no — not obviously closed under multiplication; check). The gap structure of winning C's is a 1-D sequence per p whose 'syndeticity' would be a strong structural fact.
why: If winning C's for each p are syndetic with uniformly bounded gaps (say gap ≤ G for all p ≥ p₀), then 'some C ≤ G wins' — a bounded cover, which Mordell–Schinzel suggests is false for polynomial covers but maybe true as a non-polynomial fact. The data decides.
first_step: Compute winning C ≤ 10⁵ for 100 primes near 10⁶; measure max gap; check closure properties (is C winning ⟹ kC winning for some k's?).

title: Design theory: do winning (C, a)-pairs form a block design over residue classes of p mod M?
connection: A covering design covers all k-subsets by blocks; here, blocks = {p mod M : (C, a) wins} for each (C, a); ES = covering of all prime residues. The 'covering number' structure of the block system might have a design-theoretic description (e.g. it's a union of cosets of subgroups of (ℤ/M)^×).
why: Design-theoretic regularity (each residue covered equally often) is exactly the kind of structure a uniform argument needs; irregularity points at hard residues.
first_step: For M = 840, compute for each residue r the number of (C, a) pairs with C ≤ 50 that win for ALL primes ≡ r (i.e. polynomial identities) and for a positive fraction; display as a matrix.

title: Experimental: histogram of (c, d) parameter pairs of ALL Type I solutions across primes — is the (c,d) 'mass' concentrated on few d?
connection: If most Type I solutions have d ∈ {1,2,3,5,…} small, then Type I is essentially a handful of imaginary quadratic fields; the per-d problem (class group of ℚ(√−d) fixed) is more rigid.
why: Reduces 'infinitely many (c,d)' to 'finitely many d with c varying' for the bulk of certificates — a dimension reduction for proofs.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶, tabulate the fraction of primes whose FIRST Type I solution has d ≤ 10, and the fraction with ANY d ≤ 10 solution.

title: Experimental: 'd = 1 ∪ d = 2 ∪ d = 3' — do three fixed imaginary quadratic fields already certify all primes ≤ 10⁸ (Type I)?
connection: If yes, ES on that range follows from three class-group-structured problems; the question 'is there a p with no Type I solution for d ≤ 3' becomes the sharpened target with full algebraic structure (ℤ[i], ℤ[√−2], ℤ[ω]).
why: Fixed-field problems admit Chebotarev/ray-class analysis; a fixed finite set of fields with 'all p' coverage would be a new, cleaner conjecture.
first_step: Compute for p ≤ 10⁷ whether a Type I certificate with d ∈ {1,2,3} exists (c unbounded up to p); list failures and their count growth.

title: Experimental: 'second-smallest certificate' statistics — gaps between the first and second winning parameters
connection: If the second certificate typically appears soon after the first (small ratio), solutions cluster; if far, they are 'isolated events'. Clustering suggests a local structure around certificates (a 'neighbourhood rule' generating one from another).
why: Cheap, and a neighbourhood rule would be a dynamical structure.
first_step: Compute (C₂/C₁) for the two smallest winning parameters for p ≤ 10⁶; histogram.

title: Experimental mathematics: the 'Ramanujan-style' approach — find exact identities among ES counts and classical arithmetic functions by brute-force linear algebra (Wilf–Zeilberger-free)
connection: Compute vectors (f_I(n), f_II(n), f(n), τ(n), σ(n), r₂(n), r₄(n), h(−4n), H(4n−1)…) for n ≤ 2000 and search for integer linear/bilinear relations via LLL on the data matrix. Any exact relation (even conjectural) is structural gold.
why: Standard experimental-math technique; cheap; a positive hit would redirect the campaign.
first_step: Build the matrix, run PSLQ/LLL for relations with small coefficients among ≤ 10 functions; validate hits on n ≤ 10⁵.

title: Experimental: generating-function fitting — is Σ f_II(n) q^n a quasi-modular form up to a small error?
connection: Test numerically whether the q-series of ES counts (or sub-counts) is close to a combination of Eisenstein series E₂, E₄ and theta functions: compute the coefficients, fit by least squares to a basis of modular forms of small weight/level, check residuals.
why: If a sub-count is quasi-modular, its coefficients have asymptotic formulas with explicit error (Deligne/Rankin–Selberg), potentially pointwise; a quick fit is the test.
first_step: Compute f_II(n) for n ≤ 5000; fit to the space spanned by divisor-sum functions σ_k(n), σ_k(n/2), r_k(n); report residual norm.

title: Experimental: Benford / leading-digit and last-digit statistics of certificates (a, b) to detect hidden multiplicative structure
connection: If the divisor a in 4Cp+1 = ab were 'random' among divisors, its log would be arcsine-distributed; deviations from arcsine would show the residue condition biases size (e.g. a ≈ √N preferred?).
why: Size bias reveals which divisors win — relevant to choosing weights and to Lenstra's 'large modulus ⟹ few divisors' regime.
first_step: Histogram log a / log N for all certificates of p ≤ 10⁶; compare with arcsine.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0139] Compute log(min y/p) distribution over primes ≤ 10⁸ and test for scale invariance.

title: Reverse direction: from the exceptional-prime data, construct 'ES-hard' pseudo-random primes by CRT to stress-test at 10²⁰ (profile engineering)
connection: Take the Legendre profiles of the C-form exceptions and of the adversarial primes; construct primes ≈ 10²⁰ with the same profile mod all primes ≤ 50 (CRT + primality search); measure f(p). If the profile predicts hardness, we've found a 'hardness invariant'; if not, hardness is not profile-driven.
why: Direct test of the Legendre-profile hypothesis, which underlies several items here.
first_step: Compute profiles of 409, 577, 5569, 9601 and the repo's hardest primes; CRT-construct 100 primes near 10¹⁵ per profile; compute Type I/II counts on small parameters.

title: The subset-product failure set S_C has a 'dimension' δ_C = 1 − (fraction of residue classes that can contribute): compute δ_C for all C ≤ 100 and its asymptotics
connection: For S_C defined by 'subset products of prime factors (mod 4C) avoid −1', a first-order density exponent is obtained by the largest −1-free subgroup H ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× (density of primes in H = |H|/φ(4C)); 'all factors in H' has counting function x/(log x)^{1 − |H|/φ(4C)}. The maximal −1-free subgroup has index 2 (any subgroup not containing −1 can be enlarged to index 2? Not always: in (ℤ/8)^× = {1,3,5,7}, −1 = 7; −1-free subgroups: {1}, {1,3}, {1,5} — index 2 exist ✓. In general, −1 ∉ H means H ∩ ⟨−1⟩ trivial; H can be extended to a complement of ⟨−1⟩ if the group is... (ℤ/4C)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × stuff; −1 may or may not be a 'direct summand' — e.g. in ℤ/4 (cyclic), −1 = 2 is the unique element of order 2, every nontrivial subgroup contains it! So for (ℤ/4C)^× containing a cyclic ℤ/4 summand in which −1 lies... concretely for 4C = 20: (ℤ/20)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/4 with −1 = ? ; the −1-free subgroups may have index 4.) So δ_C varies non-trivially with C — compute it.
why: δ_C controls how 'hard' it is for a prime to fail at C: small δ_C (large −1-free subgroup) = easy to fail; the C with largest δ_C are the most 'useful' certificates; a proof would use them. Possibly δ_C → 1 along C with (ℤ/4C)^× having −1 'deeply embedded' (e.g. 4C = 4q with q ≡ 1 mod 4 prime? then (ℤ/4q)^× ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/(q−1), −1 = (1, (q−1)/2); −1-free subgroups can have index 2: take {0} × ℤ/(q−1)? contains (0,(q−1)/2) ≠ −1 = (1, (q−1)/2) ✓ index 2. Hmm so index 2 always possible? Need −1 ∉ some index-2 subgroup ⟺ −1 is not a square… ⟺ some character χ mod 4C with χ(−1) = −1 (odd character) — ALWAYS exists for 4C ≥ 3. So index-2 −1-free subgroups always exist: δ_C ≤ 1/2 for all C.) So every C has δ_C = 1/2 at the top level — failure at C costs exactly (log)^{-1/2}·(const_C). Then the heuristic failure density for all C ≤ K is (log p)^{−K/2}·Π const_C, where const_C encodes the finer structure. Verify.
first_step: For C ≤ 100: list all −1-free subgroups, their indices; confirm index 2 always achievable; compute the full generating-function density of S_C (sum over all failure patterns, not just 'all in H') numerically for 4Cp+1 ≤ 10⁷.

title: ES for n = t² + 1 and n = 4t² + 1: compute identities and check whether the campaign already knows 'ES holds for all n = t² + 1'
connection: n = t² + 1: 4/(t²+1) — try x = (t²+1)/… hmm t² + 1 ≡ 1,2 mod 4; for t even n ≡ 1 mod 4. Is there a known identity? e.g. 4/(t²+1) = 1/(t²+1)·4; want 1/A + 1/B + 1/C. Note (t² + 1) + t² ... Possibly known in the literature on 'Erdős–Straus for n = polynomial values' (e.g. 'all n of the form k² + 1'?). Search.
why: If identities exist for square-avoiding polynomial families, that's an infinite family of hard-class n (not primes necessarily) — and the proof technique (polynomial in t) shows how T1 is dodged; worth 30 minutes.
first_step: git grep -il 't^2+1\|t² + 1\|k^2+1' -- '*.md'; brute-force search for identities with x, y, z ∈ ℤ[t] of degree ≤ 4 for n = t² + 1, 4t² + 1, t² + t + 1.

title: Sturmian words / Beatty sequences: the set of x with ⌊4x/p⌋ jumps, and the 'three-gap theorem' as a structure on candidate denominators
connection: The first denominator x in 4/p = 1/x + … must satisfy p/4 < x ≤ 3p/4 (for 3 terms); the candidate set and the remainders (4x − p)/(px) are governed by the Beatty-like sequence ⌊4x/p⌋; the three-gap theorem (Steinhaus) describes gap structures of such sequences — possibly organising the 'which x leaves a two-term remainder' question.
why: Structural organisation of the x-search; cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁴, mark the x in (p/4, 3p/4] whose remainder is a two-term Egyptian fraction; study the gap distribution between marked x vs three-gap predictions.

title: Compression of proofs: measure the description length of the 'certificate table' for all primes ≤ X as a function of X — the best possible 'proof length' of ES restricted to [1, X]
connection: If ES has no uniform proof, the shortest certificate table for primes ≤ X should grow like π(X)·(bits per certificate) with no compression; if a hidden uniform rule exists, compression beats this. Kolmogorov-style; measurable with real compressors on the sorted (p, C_min, a) table.
why: A direct, if crude, test for hidden uniformity, complementary to ML items.
first_step: Produce the table to 10⁷, compress with xz and with a specialised model (arithmetic coder conditioned on p mod 840); compare bits/prime to the entropy of C_min's empirical distribution.

title: Density of winning C for fixed p: is lim inf_X (1/X)#{C ≤ X : win(p, C)} > 0, and is it a continuous function of p's local data?
connection: The expected win probability per C is ≈ τ(4Cp+1)/φ(4C)-ish which → 0 as C grows… so the natural density of winning C is 0; the right normalisation is log density or weights 1/C. Σ_{C ≤ X} win(p, C)/C ≈ c(p) log X? Then c(p) is 'the ES constant of p' and ES(p) ⟺ c(p) > 0 (plus finite checks). Is c(p) an Euler product in p's local data? Compute.
why: Defines a canonical real invariant c(p) whose positivity is ES(p) with infinitely many certificates; if c(p) has an Euler-product formula (plausible: heuristically it is Σ over C-structures of local densities) then ES(p) would follow from the product's positivity — the local factors are explicit and nonzero... the catch is convergence/rigour (this is M_BM at fixed p). Still, measuring c(p) numerically and fitting an Euler product is cheap.
first_step: For 50 primes, compute Σ_{C ≤ 10⁵} win(p, C)/C vs log X; extract c(p); regress log c(p) on Legendre symbols of small primes.

title: Exceptional primes vs the 'u = 1, 2, 3 classical identities': 409 + 1 = 410 = 2·5·41 (all odd factors ≡ 1 mod 4), 411 = 3·137 (3 ≡ 3 mod 8, 137 ≡ 1), 412 = 4·103 … — build the 'residue avoidance table' for p + u, u ≤ 50, for 409 and for a random control
connection: A table showing, for each u, the prime factors of p + u mod 4u and why no subset product is ≡ −1 — the 'forensics' item in the additive form, where it is readable by hand.
why: Hand-readable evidence is the fastest route to a conjecture about the obstruction type.
first_step: Generate the table; look for the pattern (e.g., 'every odd prime factor q of p + u satisfies (q/409) = +1 or q ≡ 1 mod 4u' — a Legendre-symbol coincidence pattern).

title: ES with distinct denominators vs. allowing repeats — trivial reductions sanity table
connection: ES allows x=y; distinct version is equivalent for large n? ↔ known small cases.
why: Cheap sanity: if distinct ES fails at some p while ES holds, that's a data point about solution-set rigidity.
first_step: Compute primes ≤ 10⁷ where all solutions have a repeated denominator (expect none beyond tiny p).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Extreme value theory for max over p ≤ X of (minimal certificate size)
connection: Gumbel/Fréchet laws for maxima of iid ↔ max_p min-certificate as function of X.
why: If the max grows like (log X)^a with EVT-consistent fluctuations, extrapolate beyond 10¹⁸; deviations flag structure.
first_step: From repo census data, extract record-setting primes for 'least u in I3 word' and fit EVT growth.

title: Maximum entropy model for certificate distribution given residue constraints
connection: MaxEnt with constraints p mod q for q ≤ Q ↔ best prediction of R(p) from local data.
why: The gap between MaxEnt prediction and actual R(p) is the 'global' part; if it's small, ES difficulty is local-plus-noise.
first_step: Fit log R(p) ~ Σ_q β_q·1[p ≡ a mod q] by regularised regression and report R² vs Q.

title: Count congruences of R(p) modulo 3, 5, 8 and of partial counts R_C(p)
connection: G1 'count congruence' column: if R(p) ≢ 0 (mod m) for all p in some class, existence follows ↔ repo tested mod 2/mod 4 (fair coin).
why: Cheap scan of other moduli and of weighted/partial counts (restricted to C in a residue class, or to u ≡ B mod k) for a forced nonzero residue.
first_step: Compute R(p) and partial counts mod m for m ≤ 12 over primes p ≡ 1 mod 24 up to 10⁷; report any residue never taken (especially 0).

title: Near-miss gap g(p) = min{4/p − (1/x+1/y+1/z) > 0} and its distribution
connection: Egyptian under-approximations ↔ ES ⟺ gap 0 attainable; the minimal positive gap measures how 'close' p is to failure in a continuous sense.
why: If hard primes have systematically larger minimal positive gaps, gap-based potential functions might guide search or reveal a continuous invariant.
first_step: Compute g(p)·p³ (or appropriately normalised) for primes ≤ 10⁵ restricted to small denominators; compare hard vs easy primes.

title: First-term offset k: x = (p + 4k + 3)/4 and the binary remainder (4k+3)/(px)
connection: Choosing x = ⌈p/4⌉ + k leaves (4k+3)/(p·x) to be written as 2 unit fractions (Rav criterion: divisors d₁,d₂ of p·x with (4k+3) | d₁ + d₂) ↔ a 1-parameter family of binary problems.
why: Gives a simple 'search depth' measure k*(p); a bound k*(p) ≤ (log p)^A would be an ES-strength conjecture with a clean shape for probabilistic modelling (each k succeeds with probability ~ τ(px)/(4k+3)).
first_step: Compute k*(p) for primes ≤ 10⁸ and its max growth; model success probability per k via divisor counts of px.

title: Transport between nearby primes: 4/p = 4/q + 4(q−p)/(pq)
connection: If q close to p has a solution and the correction 4(q−p)/(pq) combines nicely ↔ continuity-type arguments (rare in arithmetic).
why: Likely dead (corrections need extra terms), but checking whether 'ES(q) + small structure ⟹ ES(p)' for q − p ∈ {4, 8, 12} ever works is cheap.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, test whether some solution of 4/q (q = p+4k prime) shares two denominators with a solution of 4/p; record frequency.

title: Correlations R(p) vs R(p + 840k): local vs global difficulty
connection: Primes in the same class mod 840 share local data ↔ if R/M is strongly correlated for p, p + 840k, difficulty is local; if not, global randomness.
why: Quantifies the 'lottery' model; complements the ML feature-importance item.
first_step: Compute correlation of R(p)/M_BM(p) and R(p')/M_BM(p') for prime pairs with p' − p = 840k, k ≤ 100.

title: Pocklington/Proth-style primality certificates as anti-certificates: when 4Cp+1 is prime, slice C fails
connection: Proth: N = k·2^n + 1 primality tests ↔ 4Cp+1 = (4C)·p + 1 is Pocklington-friendly (p | N − 1).
why: Every C with 4Cp+1 prime kills slice C; such C are certifiable cheaply. A counterexample prime p needs many such C or other failure modes; the density of 'Pocklington-prime C' for hard p is a measurable stress quantity.
first_step: Count C ≤ 10⁴ with 4Cp+1 prime for (★)-failing primes vs random primes; compare with Hardy–Littlewood prediction.

title: Universal vs per-prime certificate menus: minimal menu covering all primes in [X, 2X]
connection: Set cover over a dyadic block ↔ how menu size must grow with X (B1 says unbounded).
why: The growth law of the minimal menu (e.g. ~ log X or ~ (log X)²) is a quantitative replacement for the qualitative B1 and could be compared with the CRT-adversary cost.
first_step: Greedy set cover for primes ≡ 1 mod 24 in [10^k, 2·10^k], k = 4..8, with menu items = (u,C) pairs; fit menu size vs k.

title: No diagonal ES solutions at p ≡ 1 (mod 4): the S₃ action on solutions is free
connection: If x = y then 4/p = 2/x + 1/z forces a = 2x − p ∈ {1, p²} and 4 | p + 1, so p ≡ 3 (mod 4); same for y = z. Checked: no diagonal solution for any prime p ≡ 1 (4) below 1500; parity of the unordered count is 50/50 (scripts/z52b_signature_parity.py).
why: Freeness of S₃ means the ordered count is 6× the unordered one and kills simple involution-parity proofs (Zagier-style) — a useful negative datum for F38.
first_step: Look for a non-S₃ involution (e.g. Vieta in the hyperbola fibre) whose fixed points are classifiable; count fixed points for p ≤ 10⁵.

title: OEIS search: numbers not of the form tuv − u − v (t,u,v ≥ 2) and with 4 | t — is the sequence in OEIS?
connection: U(n)'s failure set (odd squares + {105, 2961, 3985, 25305, 111969, 978145}) is an explicit sequence; if it (or its variants) appears in OEIS, cross-references may reveal an independent characterisation.
why: OEIS cross-links occasionally reveal a known theorem behind a computed list.
first_step: Query OEIS for 105, 2961, 3985, 25305 and for the 14 (★) failure primes (409, …, 8813281).

title: Crocker's prime plus two powers of two obstruction
connection: The equation p+2^a+2^b=n has an explicit exceptional/obstruction structure (F01,F08w,F30,F33), contrasting positive-density coverage with universal coverage.
why: Its classification of failures may offer a way to search for structured ES failure families rather than only aggregate counts.
first_step: Read Crocker's construction (check whether his non-represented integers form a sparse family like 2^{2^m}−1 rather than residue classes) and compare its mechanism with the ES residue cover modulo 840 and the failed (★) primes.
refs: R. Crocker, On the sum of a prime and of two powers of two, Pacific J. Math. 36 (1971) 103–107

title: Squarefree obstruction list for xy+yz+zx
connection: OEIS A055745 is the squarefree subset of integers not represented by xy+yz+zx, sharing F25/F08w/F13 and F04: a concrete finite-looking exceptional set arises within an algebraic family and representation counts are computable.
why: Comparing obstruction types rather than just the overall existence theorem may reveal whether ES failures cluster on squarefree or squareful inputs.
first_step: Compute ES failure counts separately for squarefree n and n with square factors over a modest prime range, and compare the apparent exceptional pattern with A055745's finite-list phenomenon.

title: Uniquely represented trilinear integers as a model for witness multiplicity
connection: OEIS A093669/A093670, cross-referenced by A025052, classify numbers with a unique representation by ab+ac+bc. They share F04/F13/F14: count integral points on a symmetric cubic-form fibre, including unusually sparse one-witness fibres.
why: ES work often needs a pointwise lower bound on representation counts; the neighboring exact-one locus is a useful benchmark for how divisor factorizations control multiplicity.
first_step: For primes p, compare the number of ordered ES solutions up to permutation with the analogous factorization count on a small trilinear surface; look for a divisor-sum identity or a stable multiplicity statistic.

title: Stern primes and a second notion of additive nonrepresentation
connection: The A060003 comments identify several small exceptions as odd Stern primes, i.e. primes not of the form p+2b². This combines prime inputs with a restricted additive representation and finite exceptional values, matching F01p/F10/F25/F29.
why: Separating prime inputs from composite exceptions might reveal whether ES prime witnesses are governed by a different density or local obstruction than composite n.
first_step: Run the same candidate-generation code on ES primes and composites separately, comparing first-witness distributions and residue classes with the Stern-prime subset in A060003.

title: Strictly ordered cubic-form representations and symmetry reduction
connection: OEIS A093669 counts unique representations by ab+ac+bc under 0<a<b<c, removing permutation symmetry. It shares F04/F13/F14: a symmetric three-variable surface whose raw point count is converted to canonical unordered witnesses.
why: ES's S3 symmetry creates overcounting; the ordered-triple convention in this sequence offers an exact and transparent normalization.
first_step: For primes p, count only x≤y≤z ES triples and compare with the fully ordered count, separately tracking repeated-coordinate strata.

title: Unique-representation locus as a low-multiplicity test
connection: A093669 lists integers with exactly one strictly ordered representation as ab+ac+bc, sharing F04/F13/F25 and contrasting ES's expected polylogarithmic abundance with a rigid one-point fibre.
why: A unique-witness locus is a sensitive place to test whether an ES construction proves mere existence or can force multiple genuinely distinct solution orbits.
first_step: Enumerate ES primes with exactly one unordered solution orbit up to a modest cutoff and compare their factorization and residue signatures to the one-representation trilinear terms.

title: Addition chains: certificate search with rigorous lower bounds
connection: Addition chains match ES through F01,F32,F23,F24: finite verifiable certificates, computer searches, and a global existence/bound problem. The Scholz–Brauer problem also illustrates the gap between finding certificates and proving optimality.
why: ES witnesses are NP-style certificates; addition-chain exact-search methods could improve reproducible bounded ES searches and expose hard residue classes.
first_step: Build a bounded-depth ES certificate enumerator that canonicalizes symmetric triples and records the first uncovered prime at each depth.

title: Salez's modular filters (verification to 10¹⁷) as an explicit infinite covering family
connection: Salez found new modular equations (identity families) and used them as sieving filters to verify ES to 10¹⁷ (F23, F03, F34).
why: The filters are a concrete enumerated set of 'lines'; their combined density deficit as a function of the number of filters is an explicit covering-rate curve to compare with the Poisson model.
first_step: Extract Salez's filter list and compute the density of primes left uncovered by the first k filters for k up to 10³; fit the decay rate.

title: Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang sunflowers among minimal ES solutions → identity families
connection: ALWZ improved sunflower bounds to (log w)^{w(1+o(1))}; families of ES solutions across many n, encoded as sets of prime-power factors of (x,y,z), contain sunflowers, which correspond to shared 'cores' i.e. parametric identity families.
why: Mechanically extracts polynomial identities (Mordell-type) from solution data.
first_step: Encode the minimal solutions for primes p ≤ 10^6 in a fixed Mordell class as sets of (prime, exponent, slot) and search for sunflowers with ≥3 petals.
refs: Alweiss–Lovett–Wu–Zhang, Improved bounds for the sunflower lemma, Ann. Math. 194 (2021), arXiv:1908.08483

title: Fargues–Scholze / local Langlands — no natural ES object (recorded)
connection: Geometrisation of local Langlands (Fargues–Scholze) concerns representations of p-adic groups; ES has no evident reductive-group or Galois-representation object attached.
why: Recording the null result prevents later re-proposal; the nearest real link would go through automorphic forms attached to ES counts (theta series), which are GL₂/GL₁ and need no geometrisation.
first_step: Ask whether any ES count is a Fourier coefficient of an automorphic form on a group of rank ≥ 2; if not, close.
refs: Fargues–Scholze, Geometrization of the local Langlands correspondence, arXiv:2102.13459

title: PARI/Magma class-field computations: explicit 'ES ray class fields' for small (c,d)
connection: Computer algebra computes ray class fields explicitly; ES Type I certificates for fixed (c,d) correspond to primes f splitting in a specific ray class field with a twist by p.
why: Explicit fields allow Chebotarev-density computations of the per-(c,d) success probability, sharpening M_BM.
first_step: Compute with PARI bnrinit for d ≤ 10, c ≤ 5 and list Frobenius conditions.

title: Elkies-style 'search for structure' in large-height ES solutions via lattice reduction
connection: Elkies's ABC/Euler-conjecture searches use lattice reduction to find large solutions with structure. For ES, solutions with exceptionally large minimal x (hardest p) might be found by targeted lattice search, giving data on 'how hard' primes look.
why: It is the computational-NT native way to probe extreme cases, giving better test cases than random primes.
first_step: Search primes p < 10¹⁵ near pseudosquares for the maximal least-certificate level using lattice-guided sampling; record extremes.

title: Smoothing as a decisive ingredient: smooth weights on (u,B,C) for a weighted R_w(p)
connection: Helfgott's minor arcs only closed after choosing smoothing functions optimally. ES: replace R(p) by R_w(p) = Σ w(u,B,C)1[4uBC−u−B=p] with smooth nonnegative w; R_w(p) > 0 ⇒ ES(p).
why: Error terms in Poisson/Voronoi-based treatments of R(p) depend heavily on sharp cut-offs of the hyperbolic region; smoothing is free for a positivity statement.
first_step: Numerically compare Var_p(R_w(p)/M_w(p)) over primes near 10⁷ for sharp vs. Gaussian/Beurling–Selberg weights; pick the weight minimising the left tail.

title: Escalation of certificate menus: the ES 'truant' tree
connection: Bhargava's escalation: adjoin the smallest truant each time; finitely many escalators. ES: start with a certificate menu (Mordell identities, (★), b=1, ES₅, windows), find the least prime not covered, adjoin the cheapest family covering it, iterate; study the growth of the escalation tree.
why: Gives an empirical picture of how many families are needed up to X (B1 says bounded menus fail under Hypothesis H — the escalation rate measures how fast menus must grow).
first_step: Implement escalation over the repo's family menu up to 10⁸ and plot menu size vs. X.

title: Prime-factor census by CRT: q | 4Cp+1 iff C ≡ −(4p)⁻¹ (mod q)
connection: In Bertrand/Chebyshev the prime factorisation of a binomial coefficient is explicit. Here every prime q ∤ 2p divides 4Cp+1 exactly on one class C ≡ c_q (mod q); a single-prime certificate exists iff 4c_q | q+1 for some q ≡ 3 (mod 4) (C = c_q < q). Higher certificates combine several q's at a common C.
why: Makes the certificate problem an explicit combinatorial problem on the residues c_q(p); single-prime certificates have probability ≈ τ((q+1)/4)/q, summing to ≍ log²p — the main term in a transparent form.
first_step: Compute the single-prime-certificate count S₁(p) = #{q ≡ 3 (4) prime : 4c_q(p) | q+1} for p ≤ 10⁸ and its share of R(p); check whether S₁(p) alone ever vanishes for p in the hard list.

title: Smith-type distribution of 'certificate-free levels' in twist families
connection: Smith's method computes distributions of Selmer groups in quadratic-twist families. The set of levels C at which p has no certificate is a 'Selmer-like' local-global object varying with p; its distribution over p could be computed by Smith/Koymans–Pagano-style methods.
why: Exact distributional knowledge of the failing-level profile is stronger than the zero-law heuristics now used.
first_step: Define the profile vector (1[level C fails])_{C ≤ K} and tabulate its empirical distribution over p; compare with a product-of-local-factors model.

title: Complementary failure sets: two ES methods whose exceptions are incompatible
connection: Holowinsky's and Soundararajan's methods each fail only for forms with atypical eigenvalue statistics, in opposite directions; combined they cover every form. ES: the (★) line and the b=1 line never fail simultaneously ≤ 10⁸; find statistics S_A, S_B such that (★) failure forces S_A(p) extreme and b=1 failure forces S_B(p) extreme in an incompatible way.
why: A two-method union is an every-p proof template that does not need either method to be pointwise by itself.
first_step: Compute a battery of statistics (ℓ(p), T(p), L(1,(·/p)), M_BM, level-failure profile) for the 14 (★)-failures, the 3 b=1 failures and controls; look for anticorrelated pairs.
refs: arXiv:0809.1636 (Holowinsky-Soundararajan, Mass equidistribution for Hecke eigenforms)

title: EGZ-style reduction: from 'composite' certificates to prime-level statements
connection: EGZ for n = ab follows from EGZ for a and b by iterated extraction. ES certificates at a level 4C = 4C₁C₂: is a certificate at level C obtainable from structure at levels C₁ and C₂ (e.g. a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C₁ and one ≡ −1 mod 4C₂ combined via CRT)?
why: If levels compose, it suffices to handle prime (power) levels, where character theory is simplest.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁶ test: when 4C₁p+1 and 4C₂p+1 have certificates, does 4C₁C₂p + 1 have one more often than chance?

title: Closure maps: certificate(p) ∧ certificate(q) ⇒ certificate(r) for some r(p,q)
connection: Wilson's PBD-closure and Graham's 2n+2/2n+9 maps produce 'every large n' from finitely many seeds. ES is closed under n → kn only; search for genuinely bilinear closure operations producing certificates for new primes r from certificates of p and q.
why: Any nontrivial closure operation on certificate-carrying primes would be a completely new structural fact about ES.
first_step: Brute-force search: for pairs of (★) triples (u₁,B₁,C₁), (u₂,B₂,C₂), test small bilinear/polynomial combinations for producing triples of other primes.

title: Minimum-modulus-type statement: every certificate system covering a class must use a small modulus
connection: Hough: every distinct covering has a modulus ≤ 10¹⁶. ES analogue: for each Mordell-hard class r mod 840, any finite set of (★) congruences covering all primes in r ∩ [X, 2X] must include moduli of a certain size or divisibility (e.g. divisible by many small primes). Gives structural information on what certificates must look like.
why: Constraints on the moduli of any covering are a form of 'forced structure' usable in a proof by contradiction.
first_step: Empirically compute, for each hard class and dyadic X, the greedy minimum set of moduli covering all primes; record its smallest modulus and prime-divisibility profile.
refs: arXiv:1307.0874 (Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. Math. 181 (2015))

title: Distribution of certificates across dyadic level ranges
connection: Primes in every short interval vs almost all: the analogue at fixed p is whether certificates appear in every dyadic level range [K, 2K] (K ≤ p^{1/2}) or cluster. With R(p) ≍ log²p spread over ≍ log p dyadic ranges, ≍ log p certificates per range are expected.
why: If every dyadic range typically carries certificates, a proof could target one range of convenient size (e.g. C ≈ p^{1/3}) where tools are best; if they cluster, that range is fixed by the data.
first_step: For p ≤ 10¹⁰ in the hard list, histogram certificates by ⌊log₂ C⌋ and record the empty ranges.

title: Ramanujan-type congruences for ES counts on progressions
connection: Ramanujan/Ono congruences say p(An + B) ≡ 0 (mod m). Search for progressions An + B on which f_II(n) or R(n) is always ≡ 0 (mod m) (m = 2, 3, 4, 8) beyond the trivial evenness; such congruences would reveal modular structure that might also produce nonzero congruences at primes.
why: Systematic congruence mining is cheap and has historically uncovered hidden modular structure.
first_step: Compute f_II(n), R(n) for n ≤ 10⁷ and test all A ≤ 840, B mod A for congruences mod 2, 3, 4, 8.
refs: Ono, Ann. Math. 151 (2000) 293-307 (Distribution of the partition function modulo m)

title: Interlacing families over windows: real-rooted averages certify a good window
connection: MSS: if a family of real-rooted polynomials has a common interlacer, some member's largest root is ≤ that of the average. Define for each window e a polynomial f_e(t) (e.g. Π over prime factors q of N_e of (t − Re χ(q)) for a character χ mod e with χ(−1) = −1) whose root location detects certificates; average over e.
why: Converts 'some e works' into a statement about an averaged polynomial, which can be computed or estimated.
first_step: Construct toy f_e for small e, test interlacing numerically for hard p, and check whether the average polynomial's root implies a certificate for some e.
refs: arXiv:1304.4132 (Marcus-Spielman-Srivastava, Interlacing families I: all degrees)

title: Eventual periodicity of 'ES-easy' residue structures (Wilson-style)
connection: Wilson showed the set of orders admitting designs is eventually periodic, so finitely many residue classes need checking. For ES sub-routes, test whether 'the set of levels C at which the BM main term is positive for all p in a class r mod M' is eventually periodic in C, giving a finite description of guaranteed-positive levels.
why: Eventually periodic structures can be checked by finite computation and then fed into an every-p argument.
first_step: For M = 840, compute for each hard class r the set of C ≤ 10⁴ with M_C^lev > 0 for all p ≡ r (mod M·4C) and test periodicity in C.

title: Uncovered density of the (★) system restricted to moduli with bounded prime factors
connection: Hough's argument tracks how the uncovered set shrinks as primes are added to the moduli. Restrict ES congruences p ≡ −(u+B) (mod 4uB) to moduli 4uB built from primes ≤ y; compute the uncovered density δ(y) among integers in the hard classes and its decay in y.
why: A precise decay law for δ(y) (power of log y? exp?) quantifies how many prime 'layers' certificates need — a structural fingerprint of ES.
first_step: Compute δ(y) for y ≤ 50 by inclusion over moduli dividing a bounded smooth number, restricted to n ≤ 10⁸ in hard classes.
refs: arXiv:1307.0874 (Hough, Solution of the minimum modulus problem for covering systems, Ann. Math. 181 (2015))

title: From Tijdeman (effective finiteness) to Mihăilescu (exact): bound first, then algebra
connection: Catalan moved from 'finitely many, bounded effectively' to 'exactly one' via algebra that did not need the bound. For ES-type finiteness targets (e.g. finitely many (★)-failures), an algebraic characterisation of failures (all 14 known (★)-failures share a property P) might give the exact list without analysis.
why: The 14 known (★)-failures ≤ 10¹⁰ are a finite data set where an exact algebraic description is testable.
first_step: List the 14 primes with their factorisations of 4Cp+1 for small C, residues mod 840·k, and ℓ(p); look for a shared algebraic property and test it as a predictor above 10¹⁰.

title: Hardest residue cases needed new constructions: identify ES's 'case 3 mod 12'
connection: In Ringel–Youngs some residue classes (e.g. cases 1, 9 mod 12) took years and ad hoc ideas. Among the six Mordell-hard classes mod 840 (1, 121, 169, 289, 361, 529), measure which is hardest (lowest counts, most sub-route failures) and focus constructions there.
why: Concentrating effort on the hardest class mirrors the historical endgame.
first_step: From census data, compute per-class mean/minimum of R(p)/log²p and sub-route failure counts.

title: Sign/size arguments on special values: choose auxiliary objects whose values have forced factors
connection: Elkies chose D so that H_D(j(E)) has a controlled sign and size. ES: choose auxiliary integers built from p (values of polynomials P(p) or norms from auxiliary fields) whose sign/size/Jacobi symbol forces a prime factor in a class tied to a level C, with the factor also dividing 4Cp + 1.
why: A systematic search space for 'forcing' constructions that guarantee prime factors in classes.
first_step: Search quadratic polynomials P with P(p) | (4Cp+1)·(something) for families of C and compute Jacobi-symbol constraints on their prime factors.

title: Universality classification for the family a·tuv − b·u − c·v + d
connection: Bhargava classified universal quadratic forms by finite criteria. For the cubic family F(t,u,v) = a·tuv − b·u − c·v + d with lower bounds on t, u, v, classify which members represent every large integer (I3 is the member a = b = c = 1, d = 0, bounds ≥ 3) and find the nearest universal member to ES's constrained form.
why: Mapping the universality frontier in a family containing ES shows which constraint (4 | t, sign of d, bounds) is decisive.
first_step: Compute exception sets up to 10⁸ for small (a, b, c, d) and bounds; record which appear finite.

title: Multiplicative energy of divisor classes vs additive shifts N_e = (p + e)/4
connection: Sum-product: sets with small multiplicative energy have large sumsets. The divisor-class multisets of N_e across consecutive windows e (an additive progression in N) — compute their multiplicative energies; ES failure across many windows would force large multiplicative structure (subgroup trapping) along an additive progression.
why: Quantitative version of the sum-product incompatibility item, measurable on data.
first_step: For hard primes, compute E^×(classes of divisors of N_e mod e) for e ≤ 10³ and compare with random integers.

title: Sun-style refinements as data: four-square-like refinements of ES
connection: Sun formulated many 'refined Lagrange' conjectures by computer search; several were proved. Generate ES refinements automatically (x + y or z constrained to be a square, a prime, ≡ r mod m, etc.), test them to 10⁷, and keep those that never fail — new conjectures whose extra structure may make them provable or reveal hidden symmetries.
why: Automated conjecture generation found provable statements for sums of squares; ES has never been mined this way systematically (check repo).
first_step: Write a search over ~200 refinement predicates P(x, y, z, p) and test on all p ≤ 10⁶; report survivors.
refs: arXiv:2003.02592 (Machiavelo-Tsopanidis, Zhi-Wei Sun's 1-3-5 conjecture and variations)

title: Erdős–Vaaler-type restricted versions: ES with levels restricted to squarefree or prime C
connection: Before Duffin–Schaeffer was proved in general, restricted cases (ψ supported on special sets) were proved first. Restrict ES (★) to prime levels C (or squarefree C): the overlap structure simplifies (gcd(C, C′) = 1). Study the prime-level-only (★) failure set and its overlap model.
why: Restricted versions with clean overlap structure are the natural first targets of a Duffin–Schaeffer-type method.
first_step: Compute (★) restricted to prime C for p ≤ 10⁹ and list failures; fit an independence model.

title: Positive proportion before density one (Bourgain–Fuchs) for bounded-shape certificates
connection: Bourgain–Fuchs proved a positive proportion of integers are Apollonian curvatures before density one. For ES, bounded-shape certificate families (u, B ≤ U fixed) cover a positive proportion of primes by Dirichlet; quantify the proportion covered by shapes with u, B ≤ U as U grows, versus the full ES density one.
why: Measures how much of ES is 'explained' by bounded shapes (Mordell-type) vs growing ones — the shape-growth rate needed for density one.
first_step: Compute coverage of primes ≤ 10⁹ by (★) with u, B ≤ U for U = 1..100.
refs: arXiv:2307.02749 (Haag-Kertzer-Rickards-Stange, The local-global conjecture for Apollonian circle packings is false)
